query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A multi‐scale, first‐principles framework that independently evaluates electron-phonon coupling via DFT-based Boltzmann transport and phonon scattering via machine-learned anharmonic forcefields (explicitly accounting for oxygen-induced defect scattering) will predict the separate lattice and electronic thermal conductivities of HfNbTaTiZr with a 30–50% reduction in predictive error compared to previous conflated Debye-temperature or elastic-property-based models.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy in a bulk state with minimal oxygen contamination (≈1 wt.% or lower) and mostly ordered local environments.
generation.intervention: Apply a computational pipeline that couples DFT-derived electronic structure and Boltzmann transport for electrons with advanced anharmonic lattice dynamics based on machine-learned forcefields tailored to capture oxygen-induced defect scattering.
generation.conditions: Valid over a temperature range from below 200 K (where lattice and electronic contributions are comparable) up to 1200 K; applicable to samples with controlled minimal oxygen impurity levels.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and modified bonding environments induced by oxygen impurities, as well as the explicit electron-phonon interaction, mediate the separation of conduction channels.
generation.mechanism: By independently calculating phonon lifetimes (including defect scattering from oxygen) and electron relaxation times, the model decouples the lattice and electronic thermal transport channels. This results in a predicted gradual decline in lattice thermal conductivity at high temperatures (contrasting with sharp Debye-type drops) and, when combined with the electronic component, a total conductivity in the 10–17 W/(K·m) range.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will yield individual lattice and electronic thermal conductivity values that sum to total conductivities within 10–17 W/(K·m) at high temperatures, and will match independently measured separations at low temperatures. Compared to former approaches that conflate contributions, the predictive error is expected to be reduced by approximately 30–50%.
generation.baseline: Previous approaches relied on analytical Debye-temperature estimates, DFT-derived elastic properties, or ideal defect-free models that conflate lattice and electronic contributions, failing to capture the complexity of chemical disorder and oxygen defect effects.
generation.boundary: The prediction is restricted to well-characterized HfNbTaTiZr samples with minimal (<1 wt.%) oxygen contamination and may not hold for alloys with higher impurity levels or significantly different microstructures. The temperature applicability is limited to below ~200 K (for independent channel validation) and up to 1200 K.
generation.uncertainty: The estimated improvement of 30–50% error reduction is based on trends observed in analogous systems and simulation studies; actual predictive performance may vary due to experimental challenges in independently quantifying the two conduction channels, especially at very low temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HfNbTaTiZr samples with verified oxygen levels below 1 wt.%. Measure the thermal conductivity over a broad temperature range (from ~20 K to 1200 K) using complementary techniques. At low temperatures (<200 K), employ methods (e.g., cryogenic and magnetotransport measurements) to separately isolate lattice and electronic contributions. At high temperatures (300–1200 K), measure the total conductivity and compare with the sum of the independently predicted channels.
measurements: Spectroscopic or transport-derived estimates of phonon lifetimes and electron relaxation times
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimentally measured lattice and electronic contributions differ from the predictions by more than a 30–50% error margin (or if their sum does not fall within the expected 10–17 W/(K·m) range at high temperatures), then the hypothesis that the new predictive approach outperforms earlier models by the stated margin is falsified.

decision.trend: Early studies on concentrated and high‐entropy alloys largely relied on either simplified analytical models (e.g., Debye‐temperature based estimates) or DFT-derived elastic properties to infer thermal transport, often treating the crystal as an ideal, defect‐free medium. Subsequent work has begun to incorporate the effects of chemical disorder and lattice distortions through scaling laws and low‐frequency conductivity models, hinting at the impact of complex electron scattering and static/dynamic lattice distortions. However, these models still conflate the lattice and electronic contributions or do not account for impurity effects (such as 1 wt.% oxygen) in a unified predictive framework.
decision.unsolved: No current method provides a fully predictive approach that independently and quantitatively computes the lattice versus electronic heat transport in refractory high‐entropy alloys like HfNbTaTiZr over a broad temperature range, while also accounting for realistic defect/impurity-induced deviations from idealized behavior.
decision.lever: Develop a multi-scale, first‐principles computational framework that couples explicit electron-phonon coupling (via DFT-based Boltzmann transport for electrons) with advanced anharmonic lattice dynamics (using machine-learned forcefields tailored to capture oxygen-induced defect scattering). Key parameters include detailed phonon lifetimes, defect scattering rates, and electron relaxation times derived from ab initio downfolding of the complex disordered alloy potential.
decision.why: This approach directly addresses the longstanding issue of conflating lattice and electronic contributions by treating them as truly independent channels whose interplay is only indirectly manifested in the total conductivity. Building on the trends where earlier work incorporated lattice distortions (PMC10983832) and separately modeled electron conduction (PMC11136967) as well as the initial DFT-based approximations (PMC4735586), the new method is expected to outperform older analytical models by reducing the predictive error by an estimated 30–50%. Its validity would be confined to a temperature range below ~200 K (where lattice and electronic contributions are comparable) up to about 1200 K in samples with minimal (<1 wt.%) oxygen impurity. Decisive falsification would come from comparisons with low-temperature measurements showing that the independently computed electron and phonon contributions match experimental separations, and high-temperature data where the predicted gradual decay of lattice conductivity (versus sharp Debye-based declines) fails to reproduce total conductivity in the 10–17 W/(K m) range.
